subject.title: The Mystery of the Hunt
subject.author: Michael McClure
subject.text:
It's the mystery of the hunt that intrigues me,
                   That drives us like lemmings, but cautiously-
The search for a bright square cloud-the scent of lemon verbena-
                    Or to learn rules for the game the sea otters
                                      Play in the surf.
 
                  It is these small things-and the secret behind them
                                    That fill the heart.
                        The pattern, the spirit, the fiery demon
                                That link them together
                      And pull their freedom into our senses,
 
             The smell of a shrub, a cloud, the action of animals
 
         -The rising, the exuberance, when the mystery is unveiled.
                                 It is these small things
 
                   That when brought into vision become an inferno.

title: The Word He Spent a Lifetime Trying to Take Back
standfirst: Michael McClure once stood at his own front window and watched whalers turn carcasses into dog food. Decades later, in "The Mystery of the Hunt", he used the word for that — hunt — to describe chasing a cloud, a smell, and the sea otters he had watched come back from near the same water.

sections.heading: The Hunt He Already Knew
sections.body: Before McClure wrote a poem that uses the word "hunt" for the pursuit of a cloud, he had watched the word mean something much uglier, from his own building. Talking about this poem in a 2016 radio interview, he described the water he could see from home: "It was a pretty terrible thing to realize the whales are being caught in the bay that I could see from my front window and out to the Farallon Islands. And out there, there were boats catching whales and chopping them up and turning them into dog and cat food." That sight went straight into "For the Death of 100 Whales," the poem he read that same era at San Francisco's Six Gallery — the night Allen Ginsberg first read "Howl" to an audience. McClure's hunt, on that reading list, was the literal kind, and he loathed it.

sections.heading: A Different Answer to the Same Word
sections.body: Asked, in that same 2016 interview and specifically about this poem, what people should actually hunt for, McClure gave a short answer: "Experience. Experience of their senses and nature and each other. And beauty." The show's own framing was that the title promises killing and delivers something else — a hunt for a cloud shaped like a square, for the scent of lemon verbena, for whatever rule governs the way sea otters play in the surf. Coming from a man who had watched whales turned into pet food from his own window, that substitution does not read as a poet reaching for a vaguely outdoorsy title. It reads like someone taking a word back from what he had seen done with it, and handing it a gentler job.

sections.heading: The Otters Were an Actual Population
sections.body: The sea otters in the poem's fourth line are not a stock nature image. Southern sea otters had been hunted for fur to the point that naturalists believed the species gone from the California coast, until, on 20 June 1938, a raft of survivors was spotted off Bixby Bridge near Big Sur — an event Life magazine covered under the headline "The 'extinct' sea otter swims back to life." In the same 2016 interview, McClure said he had personally seen "the return of some of the first sea otters from Nepenthe in Big Sur," close enough to that recovery to watch it happen. So when the poem asks the reader to learn the rules of a game sea otters play, it is pointing at animals that had already survived the other kind of hunting — the kind McClure had already written a poem against.

sections.heading: Recovering "the Biological Self"
sections.body: McClure had a name for why noticing a cloud or a smell counted as serious work rather than idling. He called it recovering what he termed "the biological self." In prose examined by the scholar Rod Phillips, McClure urged readers to "THROW OUT THE WORD MAN" and take up instead "the mammalian possibility" — trusting what he called the "wisdom of the gut" as much as intellect, and refusing any split between mind and body. That is the argument underneath this poem's odd little list of hunted things. The poem's own claim is that these small things carry "the pattern, the spirit, the fiery demon / That link them together" — not decoration laid over thought, but the thing itself. For the poet whose *Ghost Tantras* (1964) abandoned English altogether for growls he called "beast language," a cloud and a scent counted as legitimate quarry because they go straight for the senses and skip the argument.

sections.heading: A Shape Borrowed From the Body
sections.body: The poem's ragged, uneven margins are not typesetting noise. McClure spent his career centering poems on the page rather than setting them flush left, a habit University of California Press describes as "center-justified, breath-based lines" — each line's length set by where a breath would end rather than by a fixed metre. Gary Snyder, who read two seats down from McClure at that same Six Gallery night, called the results "a sensitive instrument making different inventions in different poems": no fixed template, a new shape for each poem's own body. Whether that is really breath made visible, or just a looser rule than metre wearing a more persuasive justification, is a fair question the poem does not settle for you. But it is at least consistent: a piece about hunting by instinct rather than design is laid out by an instinct-based method too.
